title: Trade Liberalization and Labor Market Dynamics
research_question: How does a trade-induced sectoral price shock propagate through the labor market in the short to medium run, how long does the resulting reallocation of workers across sectors take, and how are the welfare gains and losses distributed across workers with different demographic characteristics? In addition, how effective are alternative labor market policies—such as worker retraining and moving subsidies—at compensating adversely affected workers, speeding up reallocation, and mitigating aggregate adjustment costs following trade liberalization?
data_description: The primary data source is the Relação Anual de Informações Sociais (RAIS), a Brazilian matched employer-employee administrative dataset assembled by the Ministry of Labor in which firms annually report information on the universe of formal-sector jobs. The author constructs a worker-level panel by drawing a 1% random sample of unique worker IDs (about 600,000 workers) appearing between 1995 and 2005, with prior years (1986–1994) used to build sector-specific experience as initial conditions. For each worker-year, a single job (the highest hourly-wage entry) is retained, with information on gender, age, education, hourly wage, tenure, occupation, and 5-digit industry. Industries are aggregated into four productive sectors—Agriculture/Mining, Low-Tech Manufacturing, High-Tech Manufacturing, Non-Tradeables—plus a Residual (non-formal) Sector. Aggregate value added, capital stocks, and price deflators come from the Brazilian National Accounts and IPEA.
institutional_context: Brazil underwent a major unilateral trade reform between 1988 and 1994, sharply reducing import tariffs, but tariff protection remained uneven across sectors. Tariffs in High-Tech Manufacturing stayed comparatively high in both absolute and relative terms throughout the 1990s, making it the natural import-competing sector, while Agriculture/Mining and Low-Tech Manufacturing (where Brazil holds comparative advantage given its abundance of less-skilled workers) are export-oriented. During 1995–2005, the period covered by the worker panel, employment shares shifted modestly toward Agriculture/Mining and Non-Tradeables and away from both manufacturing sectors, while substantial gross worker flows across sectors and frequent transitions in and out of formal employment coexisted with persistent inter-sectoral wage differentials. This setting—a large developing economy still adjusting to liberalization, with heterogeneous workers, sector-specific human capital, and an important informal/non-employment margin—motivates studying how trade-induced sectoral price changes reshape labor allocation and welfare.
